questions.q: The chapter groups physical infrastructure into transportation systems, utilities, communication networks and energy infrastructure. In which group does it place windmills?
questions.a: Energy infrastructure, together with solar parks and oil and gas pipelines; utilities are electricity and water pipelines.

questions.q: The chapter calls physical infrastructure a vast network of tangible structures that keep our cities and villages functioning. Which of the following is NOT physical infrastructure in this sense?
o: A farmer's knowledge of market prices
A telecom tower beside a highway
A water pipeline running to a village
A railway bridge built over a river
questions.a: A farmer's knowledge of market prices is not a tangible structure; the tower, the pipeline and the bridge are.

questions.q: The chapter opens with a quotation from APJ Abdul Kalam. According to it, a developed India will be one where
o: urban and rural areas have the same infrastructure
every large city has its own underground metro system
every district has its own international airport
every coastal state has at least one major port
questions.a: Urban and rural areas have the same infrastructure: roads, power, water and communication.

questions.q:
Match each structure shown in the chapter's pictures (Column I) with the state or union territory where it is (Column II).
Column I: 1. Muppandal Wind Farm  2. Bhakra Nangal Dam  3. Atal Setu  4. Chenab Rail Bridge
Column II: P. Himachal Pradesh  Q. Jammu and Kashmir  R. Tamil Nadu  S. Maharashtra
Choose the correct matching.
questions.a: Muppandal Wind Farm is in Tamil Nadu, Bhakra Nangal Dam in Himachal Pradesh, Atal Setu (India's longest sea bridge) in Maharashtra and the Chenab Rail Bridge in Jammu and Kashmir.

questions.q:
Assertion (A): Better infrastructure supports tourism and connects remote areas.
Reason (R): India has had a network of trade routes since ancient times.
o: Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
A is true, but R is false
A is false, but R is true
questions.a: Both are true statements from the chapter, but the ancient trade routes do not explain why infrastructure helps tourism; tourism and remote areas gain because roads, rail and air make places easy to reach.

questions.q: A bicycle factory in Ludhiana sells many more bicycles after a new highway links it to dealers in three other states. Which role of physical infrastructure named in the chapter does this show best?
o: Connecting places of manufacturing to markets
Improving access to terrain for defence forces
Helping people during floods and earthquakes
Letting citizens apply for documents online
questions.a: Transport links the place where goods are made to the markets where they are sold, which boosts trade within the country.

questions.q: (a) What does the chapter mean by physical infrastructure? (b) Give one example each of a utility and of a communication network, as the chapter lists them.
questions.a: (a) A vast network of tangible structures built to keep our cities and villages functioning. (b) Utility: electricity or water pipelines. Communication network: internet, telephone lines or telecom towers.
s: (a) A network of tangible structures that keep cities and villages functioning
(b) One correct utility and one correct communication example

questions.q: True or False: The chapter says physical infrastructure helps businesses, but it has no role in helping the government do its work. Give a reason for your answer.
questions.a: False. The chapter says physical infrastructure makes life easier for people, communities and businesses AND enables the government to function smoothly.
s: States False
Reason: it also enables the government to function smoothly

questions.q: Mohan says, 'Building networks to move goods and people is a new idea in India; nothing like it existed before modern times.' Check his claim using three facts from the chapter.
questions.a: The claim is wrong. (1) The chapter says India has had a network of trade routes since ancient times, which modern infrastructure has taken forward. (2) Kautilya's Arthashastra says the state, grama and sabhas built and maintained roads and waterways, with roads of different widths, for example 16 m for royal highways and 8 m for forest and city roads. (3) The living root bridges of Meghalaya have been nurtured over generations by the Khasi and Jaintia tribes, and some last for hundreds of years.
s: Ancient trade routes, which modern infrastructure takes forward
Arthashastra: state, grama and sabhas built and maintained roads and waterways of set widths
Living root bridges nurtured over generations, so the claim is wrong

questions.q:
A Class VII group from Pune visits a coastal town for a project. In their notebook they list what they saw: a port where ships were loading cement, a row of windmills on the hills, a mobile tower near the market, water pipelines laid along the main street to homes, and a new four-lane highway that runs from the town's factories straight to the port gates.
(a) Which two items on the list are transportation infrastructure?
(b) In which group of infrastructure does the chapter place the water pipelines?
(c) In which group does the mobile tower belong?
(d) Using the chapter, give one way the highway to the port helps the town's trade.
questions.a: (a) The port and the four-lane highway. (b) Utilities. (c) Communication networks. (d) It connects the factories where goods are made to the port, so goods reach markets inside and outside the country smoothly; the chapter says highways link with ports so goods and people travel smoothly.
s: (a) Port and highway
(b) Utilities
(c) Communication networks
(d) Links place of manufacture to the port and markets, boosting trade

questions.q: The chapter says that physical infrastructure is connected like the pieces of a puzzle. A district has good roads, steady electricity and a strong mobile network, but its canals and water pipelines have broken down, so fields get no irrigation and taps run dry for weeks. Analyse what would go wrong, and why, for each of these: (a) a tomato farmer like Satish; (b) a hospital that ambulances reach easily; (c) a school whose buses run on time; (d) a roadside eatery that serves truck drivers on the highway; (e) Finally, state in one sentence what this shows about how infrastructure works.
questions.a: (a) Without canals and pumped water there is no irrigation, so the crop fails; good roads, cold storage and the internet cannot help when there is little harvest to carry or sell. (b) Ambulances still arrive, but the hospital needs water for cleaning, treatment and patients, so care suffers. (c) Buses bring children, but with no drinking water or water for toilets the school cannot run properly and children may stay at home. (d) Trucks still pass, but the eatery cannot cook or wash dishes, so it loses customers and income. (e) The pieces of infrastructure depend on one another: one missing piece (water) weakens all the others, even when roads, power and phones work.
s: (a) No irrigation, crop fails though roads and cold storage work
(b) Ambulance arrives, but the hospital needs water to give care
(c) Buses run, but no drinking water or toilets, school suffers
(d) Eatery cannot cook or wash, loses customers despite traffic
(e) Infrastructure pieces depend on one another

questions.q: According to the chapter, where did India's road network stand in the world in 2024?
o: Third-largest, after the USA and China
questions.a: Second-largest in the world, only after the United States of America (2024).

questions.q: The Golden Quadrilateral is an important highway network. Which four cities does it connect?
questions.a: Delhi, Mumbai, Chennai and Kolkata, four of India's major cities.

questions.q: Meghalaya's living root bridges are grown from the roots of which tree?
o: Ficus elastica, the Indian rubber tree
Bamboo, grown thick along stream banks
Palm trees, whose trunks bend over streams
The banyan tree, common across the plains
questions.a: Ficus elastica, the Indian rubber tree; bamboo and palm trunks are only used to guide the roots across streams.

questions.q: Engineers must link two towns separated by a steep mountain, where a highway cannot be built along the slope. Which solution does the chapter name for such difficult terrain?
questions.a: A tunnel or a bridge: the chapter says highways cannot be built everywhere, and in steep mountains, dense forests and wide river beds, bridges and tunnels give ease of access.

questions.q:
Consider the following statements about roads in India.
I. Local roads help farmers carry crops to markets and ambulances reach hospitals.
II. National highways and expressways connect with railway stations, airports and ports so that goods and people can travel smoothly.
III. NH44, the longest national highway in India, connects Delhi, Mumbai, Chennai and Kolkata.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
questions.a: I and II only. Statement III is wrong: NH44 runs from Srinagar in the north to Kanyakumari in the south; it is the Golden Quadrilateral that connects Delhi, Mumbai, Chennai and Kolkata.

questions.q: (a) Name the longest national highway in India and give its length. (b) Name the places at its northern and southern ends.
questions.a: (a) NH44, 4,112 km long. (b) Srinagar in the north and Kanyakumari in the south.
s: (b) Srinagar to Kanyakumari

questions.q: True or False: Expressways are built and maintained by the state public works departments, because they join cities within one state. Give the correct statement.
questions.a: False. Expressways and national highways join cities across states and are built and maintained by the central government; state public works departments build state highways that connect towns and districts within a state.
s: States False
Corrects it: expressways and national highways join cities across states and are built by the central government

questions.q: Answer briefly about Meghalaya's living root bridges. (a) Which communities craft them, and what do they use to guide the roots across streams? (b) How long do they take to mature, and how long can they last? (c) State one cultural meaning the chapter gives them.
questions.a: (a) The indigenous Khasi and Jaintia tribes; they guide the roots with bamboo and palm trunks. (b) Some take decades or even centuries to mature and can last for hundreds of years. (c) They connect one generation to another and reflect the local people's knowledge of Nature.
s: (a) Khasi and Jaintia; bamboo and palm trunks
(b) Decades or centuries to mature; last hundreds of years
(c) Connect one generation to another / reflect knowledge of Nature

questions.q:
Two hill towns are separated by a steep mountain. The only road goes over a high pass; the journey takes 5 hours, and snow closes the pass for 4 months every year. The state can pay for only ONE project:
Project P: widen the pass road, so the journey takes 4 hours, but snow will still close it for 4 months.
Project Q: dig a tunnel through the mountain, so the journey takes 2 hours and stays open all year.
(a) For how many months a year is the pass road open now?
(b) How many hours does Project Q save on one journey compared with Project P?
(c) According to the chapter, in which three kinds of terrain can highways not be built everywhere, and what enables ease of access there?
(d) Which bridge in the chapter gave year-round travel where the earlier way of crossing failed in one season? Name the crossing it replaced.
(e) Which project should the state choose? Justify your decision using your answers to (a) and (b) and one benefit the chapter gives for year-round travel.
questions.a: (a) 12 - 4 = 8 months. (b) 4 - 2 = 2 hours. (c) Dense forests, wide river beds and steep mountains; bridges and tunnels enable ease of access there. (d) The Dhola Sadiya Bridge (Bhupen Hazarika Setu); it replaced ferries, which did not work during floods. (e) Project Q: it is open for all 12 months instead of only 8, and it is 2 hours shorter than the widened road (3 hours shorter than today). As with the Dhola Sadiya Bridge, year-round travel lets farmers take vegetables and fruits to market before they spoil and lets people reach hospitals or medicines faster, even in the bad season.
s: (a) 8 months
(b) 2 hours
(c) Dense forests, wide river beds, steep mountains; bridges and tunnels
(d) Dhola Sadiya Bridge; it replaced ferries that failed in floods
(e) Chooses Q, citing 12 vs 8 months and 2 hours saved, plus one benefit (produce reaches market before spoiling or faster hospital access)

questions.q:
Sharma Transport in Delhi runs trucks to three other big cities: Mumbai, Chennai and Kolkata. All three routes use one highway network that joins these four cities. At the end of each trip the trucks drive into a port or a railway goods yard. The owner notes that the Delhi to Mumbai trip of about 1,400 km takes 35 hours of driving.
(a) Name the highway network the trucks use.
(b) Which government builds and maintains national highways?
(c) Find the average driving speed on the Delhi to Mumbai trip.
(d) The owner says, 'National highways matter only for trucks that go long distances.' Using the chapter, give one reason why this is not the full picture.
questions.a: (a) The Golden Quadrilateral. (b) The central government. (c) 1,400 / 35 = 40 km per hour. (d) The chapter says national highways and expressways connect with railway stations, airports and ports so that goods AND people travel smoothly; they join cities across states for passengers too, not only long-distance trucks.
s: (a) Golden Quadrilateral
(b) Central government
(c) 1,400 / 35 = 40 km per hour
(d) Highways link with stations, airports and ports for goods and people

questions.q: In which year did the British introduce railways in India?
questions.a: 1853, to carry raw materials like cotton and tea to ports for export to Britain.

questions.q: The chapter's timeline of trains in India shows the WDM-1 locomotive of 1957. What kind of locomotive was it?
questions.a: A diesel locomotive; the F-734 (1895) was steam, the WAM-4 (1970) electric, and the Vande Bharat (2019) is an electric train.

questions.q:
Assertion (A): Metro trains help lower pollution in cities.
Reason (R): Metro trains run on underground and elevated tracks, which cuts travel time.
o: Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
A is true, but R is false
A is false, but R is true
questions.a: Both are true, but the tracks explain why metros cut travel time. Metros lower pollution because they use cleaner fuels like electricity, some even solar power, as the Delhi Metro does.

questions.q: In a busy city, office workers spend over an hour in traffic jams each morning. Which feature of metro trains, as the chapter describes it, most directly cuts their travel time?
o: Running on underground and elevated tracks
Using solar power, like the Delhi Metro
Being one of the cheapest services in the world
questions.a: Running on underground and elevated tracks keeps metros out of road traffic, so they cut travel time; solar power lowers pollution, not travel time.

questions.q: (a) Where does Indian Railways stand among the railway systems of the world? (b) Name two kinds of indirect jobs the railways create.
questions.a: (a) It is the fourth-largest railway system in the world. (b) Any two of catering, vending and taxi services.
s: (a) Fourth-largest in the world
(b) Two of catering, vending, taxi services

questions.q: True or False: Earlier, trains in India ran on coal and diesel, which caused a lot of pollution. Say what India is now doing about it.
questions.a: True. India is now aiming to have 100 per cent of its trains running on electricity, which is better for the environment.
s: States True
India aims for 100 per cent electric trains, better for the environment

questions.q: State three changes that came about as the railway network expanded in India.
questions.a: (1) Trade grew. (2) Major markets developed. (3) New settlements emerged near railway stations. (Railways became a lifeline for moving people and goods.)
s: Trade grew
Major markets developed
New settlements emerged near stations

questions.q: Fig. 7.8 gives the percentage of each country's railway network that was electrified in 2024: India 97, China 75, France 61, Germany 55, United Kingdom 38. Divya writes, 'Adding China, France and Germany gives 191, so those three together have about twice as many kilometres of electric track as India.' Is her reasoning correct? Explain, and say what the figure does show.
questions.a: No. Each number is a percentage of that country's OWN network, not a length in kilometres, so percentages of different countries cannot be added to compare track lengths (75 + 61 + 55 = 191 means nothing in km). The figure shows that India has electrified the largest share of its network (97 per cent) of the five countries; for example 97 - 61 = 36 percentage points more than France.
s: Says the reasoning is wrong
Explains that the figures are percentages of each country's own network, not km, so they cannot be added
States what it shows: India has the highest share electrified

questions.q: Your class is making a fact card on metro trains in India for the school notice board. Write one line under each heading: (a) number of cities and total length of the network; (b) where India's metro network will soon rank in the world; (c) two benefits for daily commuters; (d) how metros lower pollution, with the chapter's example.
questions.a: (a) Metros run in 23 Indian cities, over 1,000 km in all. (b) Soon the third-largest network in the world, after China and the USA. (c) Any two: fast and reliable travel, easier daily commutes, less road traffic, shorter travel time. (d) They use cleaner fuels like electricity, and some even use solar power, like the Delhi Metro.
s: (a) 23 cities, over 1,000 km
(b) Soon third-largest, after China and the USA
(c) Two benefits for commuters
(d) Electricity; Delhi Metro uses solar power

questions.q: Analyse how Indian Railways today help the country in five different ways. Use one fact or figure from the chapter for each way.
questions.a: (1) Moving people: they carry over 20 million passengers every day. (2) Cheap travel: they are one of the cheapest train services in the world. (3) Moving goods with less energy: cargo trains carry coal, grains, textiles and electronics using 75 to 90 per cent less energy than road transport. (4) Cleaner environment: India aims for 100 per cent electric trains, and 97 per cent of the network was electrified in 2024. (5) Jobs: Indian Railways is the largest employer with about 1.21 million employees in 2024, and creates indirect jobs in catering, vending and taxi services.
s: Passengers: over 20 million a day
One of the cheapest train services
Cargo trains use 75-90 per cent less energy than road
Electrification (97 per cent in 2024 / aim of 100 per cent)
Jobs: about 1.21 million employees plus indirect jobs

questions.q: How many airports did India have in 2025, according to the chapter?
questions.a: 159 airports in 2025.

questions.q: Which pair of goods would the chapter expect cargo flights to carry?
questions.a: Vaccines and seafood: cargo flights move high-value or perishable goods such as vaccines, chemicals and seafood; ships and cargo trains carry the heavy goods.

questions.q:
Match each mode of transport in Column I with what the chapter says it carries in Column II.
Column I: 1. Ships  2. Cargo flights  3. Cargo trains  4. Metro trains
Column II: P. Daily commuters inside a city  Q. Heavy goods like cars and cement over long distances  R. Grains, textiles and electronics on land  S. High-value or perishable goods like vaccines
Choose the correct matching.
questions.a: Ships carry heavy goods like cars and cement over long distances; cargo flights carry high-value or perishable goods such as vaccines; cargo trains carry grains, textiles and electronics; metros carry daily city commuters.

questions.q:
Consider the following statements.
I. Air transport is the cheapest way to move heavy goods over long distances.
II. India has 12 major ports and 217 minor ports.
III. The volume of cargo handled at India's ports fell by 50 per cent in the past decade.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
questions.a: II only. Statement I is wrong: air is the fastest mode, while ships are the cheaper mode for heavy goods. Statement III is wrong: cargo volume INCREASED by 50 per cent in the past decade.

questions.q:
Assertion (A): Air transport is particularly helpful in delivering aid to people during floods and earthquakes.
Reason (R): Aircraft can easily reach difficult terrains such as high mountains, deserts, dense forests and long oceanic stretches.
o: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true, but R is false
A is false, but R is true
questions.a: Both are true and R explains A: aircraft reach places that roads cannot reach after a disaster, which is why the chapter calls air transport helpful for disaster aid.

questions.q: Fig. 7.21 gives the container trade of some world ports in 2024 in million TEU: Shanghai 51.51, Singapore 41.12, Mumbai 7.05. About how many times Mumbai's volume did Singapore handle?
questions.a: 41.12 / 7.05 is about 5.8, so about 6 times. (34 is the difference 41.12 - 7.05, not a ratio; about 7 times is Shanghai's figure.)

questions.q: True or False: India's long coastline is connected to regions such as West Asia, Africa and Europe, and this supports trade through shipping. Give one reason ships are used for such trade.
questions.a: True. Ships are a cheaper mode of transport and carry heavy goods like coal, cars and cement over long distances.
s: States True
Ships are cheaper and carry heavy goods over long distances

questions.q: State three ways in which air transport helps people and businesses, as given in the chapter.
questions.a: (1) It is the fastest way to connect people and places within and across countries (passenger flights). (2) Cargo flights move high-value or perishable goods such as vaccines, chemicals and seafood. (3) It helps deliver aid during disasters like floods or earthquakes, reaching high mountains, deserts, dense forests and long oceanic stretches.
s: Fastest way to connect people and places
Cargo flights carry high-value or perishable goods
Delivers aid in disasters to difficult terrain

questions.q:
A travel magazine writes about flying in India. It reports that Indian airports handled around 376 million passengers in 2024-25 and that the country had 159 airports in 2025. Suppose two big city airports together handled 140 million of those passengers. The editor wants a line saying where India stands in the world for domestic air traffic, and a short comment on a state plan to build a small airport in a remote hill district that is often cut off by landslides.
(a) Where does India rank in the world for domestic air traffic, and after which countries?
(b) What percentage of all the passengers did the two city airports handle, to the nearest whole number?
(c) A reader says, 'These two airports handle more than half of India's air passengers.' Is the reader right? Use the numbers to decide.
(d) Should the state build the hill-district airport? Give a justified judgement using what the chapter says about air transport.
questions.a: (a) Third-highest, after the USA and China. (b) 140 / 376 x 100 = about 37 per cent. (c) No: 37 per cent is less than half; the other 157 airports together handled 376 - 140 = 236 million passengers, about 63 per cent. (d) Yes, with care: air transport is the fastest mode and can reach difficult terrain like high mountains, so an airport would bring aid, medicines and people in when landslides cut the roads, and would also support tourism; the state should weigh this against the cost, but for a district often cut off the safety benefit is strong.
s: (a) Third-highest, after the USA and China
(b) 140 / 376 x 100 = about 37 per cent
(c) Not right: 37 per cent is under half; the other airports handled 236 million (about 63 per cent)
(d) Justified judgement using air reaching difficult terrain and disaster aid

questions.q: Make a five-line fact sheet titled 'India's Ports and Shipping' for your class. Write one line on each: (a) the approximate length of India's coastline; (b) the regions it is connected to for trade; (c) three heavy goods that ships carry; (d) the number of major and minor ports; (e) how the volume of cargo handled has changed in the past decade.
questions.a: (a) About 11,100 km. (b) West Asia, Africa and Europe. (c) Coal, cars and cement. (d) 12 major ports and 217 minor ports. (e) It has increased by 50 per cent.
s: (a) About 11,100 km
(b) West Asia, Africa, Europe
(c) Coal, cars, cement
(d) 12 major and 217 minor ports
(e) Increased by 50 per cent

questions.q: In which year was India's first printed newspaper, the Bengal Gazette, brought out?
questions.a: 1780; 1605 is the first newspaper printed in Germany, 1844 the telegraph and 1930 the start of AIR broadcasting.

questions.q: The chapter lists the parts of communication infrastructure that lie behind our phones and computers. Which of the following is NOT one of them?
questions.a: Cold storage units keep farm produce fresh; communication infrastructure includes cables, wireless devices, towers, satellites and data centres.

questions.q:
Match each year in Column I with the event from the chapter's communication timeline in Column II.
Column I: 1. 1780  2. 1930  3. 1993  4. 1994
Column II: P. All India Radio broadcasting started in India  Q. India's first printed newspaper, the Bengal Gazette  R. First version of the smartphone developed  S. Internet and the World Wide Web
Choose the correct matching.
questions.a: 1780 Bengal Gazette; 1930 AIR broadcasting began; 1993 first version of the smartphone; 1994 the internet and the World Wide Web.

questions.q:
Assertion (A): J.C. Bose's inventions did not gain the international recognition they deserved, although he received several honours.
Reason (R): Bose rarely bothered to patent his inventions.
o: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true, but R is false
A is false, but R is true
questions.a: Both are true and R explains A: the chapter says that not patenting his inventions did not help them gain international recognition.

questions.q: A resident photographs a broken streetlight and files a complaint with the municipal office through its mobile app, without visiting the office. Which use of communication infrastructure named in the chapter does this show?
o: Emergency response through quick SMS alerts
questions.a: E-governance: the chapter says communication lets citizens apply for documents, file complaints or get information easily from the government.

questions.q:
Consider the following statements about J.C. Bose.
I. In 1895, in an experiment in Calcutta, he showed that signals could pass through a wall.
II. Guglielmo Marconi patented a similar device in 1901 and won the Nobel Prize in Physics in 1909.
III. Bose created the Bose Institute in 1917.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
questions.a: All three are correct as the chapter states them.

questions.q: (a) What is e-commerce, according to the chapter? (b) What is a patent?
questions.a: (a) Buying or selling products and services on online platforms or over the internet. (b) A right granted by the government or institutions to be the only person or company who can make, sell or use an invention for a certain number of years.
s: (a) Buying or selling on online platforms / the internet
(b) Right to be the only one to make, sell or use an invention for some years

questions.q: (a) Name the invention of 1844 that sent messages over long distances using dots and dashes, and its inventor. (b) How was it different from the way messages travelled between 200 BCE and 1200 CE?
questions.a: (a) The telegraph, invented by Samuel Morse. (b) It sent an electric signal, while earlier messages had to be carried physically by pigeons, runners and horse couriers, which was much slower.
s: (a) Telegraph, Samuel Morse
(b) Electric signal versus messages carried by pigeons, runners, horse couriers

questions.q: Raghav says, 'Before All India Radio started, there was no way to send a message quickly over a long distance.' Check his claim using three entries from the chapter's communication timeline, with their years.
questions.a: The claim is wrong. AIR broadcasting started in 1930, but long before that: (1) in 1844 the telegraph sent electric signals over long distances; (2) in 1876 Alexander Graham Bell invented the telephone; (3) in 1899 J.C. Bose demonstrated wireless transmission (and the fax machine of 1843 sent images).
s: Telegraph 1844
Telephone 1876
Bose wireless 1899 or fax 1843, so the claim is wrong

questions.q: The chapter says progress in communication infrastructure has promoted ease of living. Analyse this for four areas of life: (a) education, (b) disasters, (c) business, (d) government services. For each, give one example from the chapter and say how it makes life easier.
questions.a: (a) Education: online classes, digital libraries and educational videos reach students even in remote areas, so they learn without travelling to a city. (b) Disasters: quick SMS alerts or apps warn people early so they can move to safety. (c) Business: small and large businesses sell across the world through e-commerce and receive quick online payments, so they reach more buyers. (d) Government services: through e-governance citizens apply for documents, file complaints or get information online, for example storing an Aadhaar card in DigiLocker, saving trips to offices.
s: (a) Online classes / digital libraries for remote students
(b) SMS alerts or apps in disasters
(c) E-commerce and online payments for businesses
(d) E-governance, e.g. DigiLocker, saves trips to offices

questions.q:
Lakshmi weaves cotton saris in a small town in Telangana. She used to sell about 15 saris a month at the weekly market. Last year a cousin helped her put photographs of her saris on a shopping website, and in the first three months she received 45 orders from buyers in other states, paid through quick online payments. Each order is sent by courier after a message reaches her phone through the nearby mobile tower.
(a) What does the chapter call buying and selling of this kind?
(b) Name two parts of communication infrastructure, other than the two phones, that carry a buyer's order message to Lakshmi.
(c) On average, how many online orders did she get a month, and how many saris did she sell a month in all, if the market sales stayed the same?
(d) Lakshmi's neighbour says that now the weekly market no longer matters to her business. Is the neighbour right? Decide using your answer to (c).
questions.a: (a) E-commerce. (b) Any two of: the mobile tower (powered by electricity), fibre cables, satellites, servers in data centres. (c) 45 / 3 = 15 online orders a month; 15 + 15 = 30 saris a month in all, double her earlier sales. (d) No: the weekly market still sells 15 of her 30 saris a month, which is half (50 per cent) of her sales, so it still matters as much as the website.
s: (a) E-commerce
(b) Two of tower, fibre cables, satellites, servers/data centres
(c) 15 a month online, 30 in all
(d) Not right: market gives 15 of 30 saris, half her sales

questions.q: Which of the following does the chapter call social infrastructure?
questions.a: A fire station; social infrastructure includes schools, hospitals, police and fire stations, courts, parks, libraries and community centres, while the others are physical infrastructure.

questions.q:
Assertion (A): According to the Arthashastra, roads leading to villages were to be as wide as royal highways.
Reason (R): The Arthashastra suggested a severe penalty for those who broke the dam of a reservoir.
o: Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
A is true, but R is false
A is false, but R is true
questions.a: Both are true, but R does not explain A: both royal highways and roads leading to villages were to be 16 m wide, while the penalty for breaking a dam is about deterring damage to waterworks, not about road widths.

questions.q:
Consider the following statements about infrastructure in Kautilya's Arthashastra (measurements simplified to metres).
I. Royal highways and roads leading to villages were to be 16 m wide.
II. Forest roads were to be wider than royal highways.
III. The upkeep of roads and waterways was left to the state alone.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
questions.a: I only. Statement II is wrong: forest roads were 8 m, narrower than the 16 m royal highways. Statement III is wrong: the state, grama and sabhas were all involved.

questions.q: True or False: The chapter says the design of infrastructure should consider the needs of children, the elderly and disabled persons. Give one example of such design from the chapter's pictures.
questions.a: True. The chapter shows elderly-friendly transport systems designed for smooth mobility (Fig. 7.29).
s: States True
Example: elderly-friendly transport for smooth mobility

questions.q: (a) Name two Panchayat or municipal services that the chapter says need to be improved. (b) In a town where lanes overflow with sewage every monsoon and people fall ill, which one service should be improved first? Give a reason.
questions.a: (a) Any two of: waste management, sewer systems, traffic management, clean and safe drinking water, pedestrian-friendly footpaths. (b) Sewer systems, because overflowing sewage is the cause of the illness and blocks the lanes; fixing it protects health and ease of living first.
s: (a) Two services from the chapter's list
(b) Sewer systems, with a reason tied to the sewage problem

questions.q:
A new railway line will run through a forest where elephants cross the track at 12 places. Two plans cost the same.
Plan A: alarm systems at all 12 crossings, with electric trains and solar panels on the station buildings.
Plan B: alarm systems at only 5 crossings, with diesel engines and a faster track.
(a) At how many crossings would Plan B leave animals without a warning?
(b) Which plan fits the chapter's idea of safe and sustainable infrastructure?
(c) Justify your choice with two points from the chapter.
questions.a: (a) 12 - 5 = 7 crossings. (b) Plan A. (c) The chapter shows alarm systems used when animals cross railway tracks, and Plan A protects animals (and trains) at every crossing, not just 5; it also uses cleaner energy, since solar panels for buildings reduce emissions, and sustainable infrastructure should minimise pollution and harm to biodiversity. Plan B's faster track does not make up for 7 unprotected crossings.
s: (a) 7 crossings
(b) Plan A
(c) Alarms at all crossings protect animals; cleaner energy/solar reduces emissions and harm to biodiversity

questions.q: A town council has money for only one project this year. Plan 1 is a new flyover in the town centre. Plan 2 is to improve waste management, sewers and pedestrian-friendly footpaths in all wards. (a) Which plan matches the services the chapter says Panchayats and municipalities must improve? (b) Give two reasons from the chapter that support Plan 2. (c) Give one fair point in favour of Plan 1. (d) State one design condition from the chapter that either project must meet. (e) Make your recommendation and justify it.
questions.a: (a) Plan 2: waste management, sewer systems and pedestrian-friendly footpaths are in the chapter's list of services to improve. (b) Littered roads and poor waste management reduce ease of living and become a burden for every citizen; footpaths and clean surroundings serve everyone, including children and the elderly. (c) A flyover can ease traffic in the town centre; the chapter lists traffic management as a service too, and good roads help goods and people move. (d) It must be safe and sustainable, using cleaner energy and environment-friendly materials, and consider the needs of children, the elderly and disabled persons. (e) A reasoned choice, for example Plan 2, because it reaches every ward and every citizen's daily life, while the flyover helps mainly the centre; Plan 1 is acceptable if justified by severe traffic.
s: (a) Plan 2 matches the chapter's list
(b) Two reasons: ease of living, burden on citizens, serves all
(c) One fair point for the flyover
(d) Safe, sustainable and inclusive design condition
(e) Justified recommendation

questions.q:
The residents' welfare association of Gulmohar Colony runs a public park. In one month the caretaker finds six places where people broke the hedge to get in, writing on the boundary wall, and 40 bags of litter. Cleaning costs the association Rs 150 for each bag, paid from every family's monthly fee. One member wants a fine for anyone caught damaging the park; another says fines alone are enough, because the money collected from fines will pay for the cleaning.
(a) Is a public park physical infrastructure or social infrastructure, according to the chapter?
(b) What did Kautilya's Arthashastra recommend for people who trespassed into public parks by breaking the hedge?
(c) Find the month's cleaning cost and explain, using the chapter, why such damage is a burden for every resident.
(d) Are fines alone enough? Give a justified judgement using the chapter.
questions.a: (a) Social infrastructure (parks are in the chapter's list with schools, hospitals and libraries). (b) Fines. (c) 40 x 150 = Rs 6,000, paid from every family's fee; the chapter says damage to public infrastructure reduces ease of living and becomes a burden for every citizen. (d) No. Fines can deter damage and may pay for some cleaning, but they do not stop all damage or mend a broken hedge. The chapter says that while penalties deter damage, the role of citizens is equally important: residents must use the park responsibly and report damage to the authorities, because taking care of public infrastructure is a collective responsibility.
s: (a) Social infrastructure
(b) Fines for trespassing by breaking the hedge
(c) Rs 6,000; damage is a burden for every citizen
(d) Fines deter, but citizens must use responsibly and report: collective responsibility
